title: Dal Chawal Goes to the James Beard Awards: An Indian-American Dietitian's Mission to Feed America Its Humblest Meal
excerpt: Sapna Punjabi's debut cookbook — 85 vegetarian recipes celebrating lentils and rice — has been nominated for a 2026 James Beard Book Award, with a vision that stretches from the kitchen shelf to hospital cafeterias.
body:
There is a meal that every Indian knows by heart. It requires no recipe card, no YouTube tutorial, no dinner-party ambition. It is dal and rice — *dal chawal* — the two-ingredient anchor of a civilisation's daily eating. And this month, it will be celebrated at the Art Institute of Chicago when the James Beard Foundation announces its 2026 Book Awards on June 13.

*Dal Chawal: 85 Vegetarian Indian Recipes Combining the Power of Dal and Rice* by Sapna Punjabi has been nominated in the Vegetable-Focused Cooking category, placing India's most elemental comfort food alongside the year's best plant-based cookbooks from around the world. Published by Hardie Grant Books, the slim but ambitious volume is the debut work of a Mumbai-born, Irving, Texas-based registered dietitian who has spent two decades quietly building a case that dal chawal is not just soul food — it is science.

## A Dietitian's Kitchen

Punjabi's path to the James Beard stage is unusual. She is not a celebrity chef or a food-media personality. She trained as a clinical dietitian in Mumbai, then moved to the United States in the late 1990s, arriving in Ohio during a snowstorm with a pressure cooker packed in her luggage by her mother. She worked for years as a neonatal dietitian in American hospitals before founding beSPICED, a culinary wellness-spice brand that marries Ayurvedic principles with Western nutritional science.

The cookbook grew from that intersection. Each recipe — from shalgam wali dal (turnip lentils from Kashmir) to kumbakonam kadappa (a tangy Tamil Nadu specialty) — is annotated with its Ayurvedic properties alongside its macronutrient profile. Chapters are organised by lentil variety: moong, masoor, chana, toor, and urad, each treated with the seriousness that Western cookbooks reserve for cuts of meat or varietals of tomato.

"For any Indian, dal chawal is more than a meal of pulses and rice," wrote Vikas Khanna, the Michelin-starred chef, in his endorsement of the book. "It holds a deep emotional connection and is a keeper of family memories, traditions, and culture on a plate."

## The Complete Protein Argument

Punjabi's central thesis is deceptively simple: dal and rice together form a complete protein. The amino acids missing from one are present in the other, creating a nutritional profile that rivals animal protein at a fraction of the cost — and without the environmental footprint. It is a fact that nutritionists have known for decades, but one that has never been communicated to mainstream America in a way that is appetising rather than academic.

The recipes were tested repeatedly with feedback from friends and colleagues of different ethnicities — a deliberate choice. "I wanted this book to work for any kitchen, not just an Indian one," Punjabi has said. The result is a collection that respects tradition while remaining accessible: handvo (a Gujarati savoury cake) sits alongside chakkara pongal (a sweet South Indian rice dish), with each recipe's spice quantities calibrated for American grocery stores.

## Beyond the Bookshelf

What sets Punjabi apart from the growing shelf of Indian cookbooks in America is her stated long-term goal: she wants to put dal chawal into institutional food service. Hospitals. Schools. University dining halls. The places where Americans actually eat most of their meals but where Indian food remains almost entirely absent.

It is a radical ambition dressed in pragmatic clothing. Dal is cheap, shelf-stable, and endlessly variable. Rice is already a staple in cafeteria kitchens. Together, they address the twin crises of nutrition and food cost that American institutions face daily. And unlike many plant-based alternatives that require exotic ingredients or specialised equipment, dal chawal can be made with a single pot and pantry staples.

## A Growing Shelf

Punjabi's nomination arrives at a moment when Indian food writing is enjoying unprecedented recognition in America. The same James Beard ceremony will honour *MUMBAI: A Journey Through Its Kitchens, Streets, and Stories* by Rushina Munshaw Ghildiyal in the Visuals category, while multiple Indian-origin chefs and restaurateurs are finalists in the Restaurant and Chef Awards.

James Beard Award finalist Nik Sharma praised the book for "confidently filling the gap in the conversations around Ayurvedic foods and cooking." Ellie Krieger, the PBS host and James Beard-winning author, called it a guide that "will open your eyes to the kaleidoscope of possibilities for these staple ingredients."

For the millions of NRIs who grew up eating dal chawal every day — and who now feed their American-born children versions of it in kitchens from Fremont to Frisco to Flushing — the nomination carries a weight that transcends literary prizes. It is an acknowledgement that the meal they have always known as essential, complete, and deeply satisfying is finally being seen that way by the country they call home.

The awards ceremony takes place on June 13 at the Art Institute of Chicago.
